You have a Senior Executive Service (SES) role in mind, but the vacancy hasn’t opened. Maybe you’re a GS-14 or GS-15 federal leader already directing a program, managing people, or overseeing a substantial budget. You know the work you’ve done. The harder part is deciding which accomplishments belong on a two-page SES resume and how to show that your experience matches the agency’s needs.

Start with a past announcement for a comparable role and a list of leadership decisions you can explain in detail. Those two pieces will give you a head start on your SES application and show you where you still need stronger evidence.

1. Use a comparable SES vacancy to identify what the agency needs

Look for a prior USAJOBS announcement for the same role or a similar federal executive position. Read the duties first. What would the incoming executive be responsible for delivering? Would they inherit a modernization initiative, oversee regional operations, or improve a program under scrutiny?

Then review the qualifications and required documents. Note the Executive Core Qualifications (ECQs) and any Mandatory Technical Qualifications (MTQs) or Mandatory Technical Competencies (MTCs) listed. A comparable announcement gives you a working target. When the vacancy opens, use the live posting to confirm eligibility, qualifications, supporting documents, and the application deadline. See a USAJOBS SES announcement for an example.

Make a simple worksheet with three columns: the agency requirement, your best example, and the evidence you can verify. If the role calls for leading operations across multiple locations, record the sites and teams you oversaw, the problem you were accountable for, and what improved under your leadership. A blank column tells you what to research before you start writing.

2. Match your accomplishments to the current Executive Core Qualifications

The U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM) lists five Executive Core Qualifications for entry to the Senior Executive Service. Use the current list to sort your experience. Review OPM’s Executive Core Qualifications.

Executive Core QualificationEvidence to look for in your experience
Commitment to the Rule of Law and the Principles of the American FoundingA leadership decision that upheld a legal obligation or strengthened accountability in delivering a public service
Driving EfficiencyA change you led that improved how your organization used its budget, staffing, or technology
Merit and CompetenceA complex problem you solved by applying sound judgment and relevant expertise under pressure
Leading PeopleA time you developed managers, set clearer expectations, or led teams through a difficult change
Achieving ResultsA priority you translated into action, with a measurable result tied to the agency’s mission

For each example, record what you personally decided, who helped implement it, and how you measured the outcome. Use figures you can substantiate and are authorized to share. The strongest example is the one that shows how your decision affected an outcome the hiring agency cares about.

3. Use CCAR to turn a responsibility into a leadership accomplishment

The Challenge, Context, Action, and Result (CCAR) framework helps you unpack an accomplishment before you write a resume bullet or practice for an SES interview. Here’s a fictional example.

Responsibility: Oversaw operations and coordinated process improvements across regional offices.

SES resume accomplishment: Directed a case review redesign across six regional offices, leading 12 managers in setting common triage criteria and reallocating staff to high-backlog locations. Cut the backlog by 28% in nine months while maintaining audit compliance.

That revision gives the reader the scope, the executive action, and the result. In your working notes, keep the fuller story. Capture what caused the backlog, why you chose to reallocate staff, and how you verified the improvement. Those details give you material for interview questions about tradeoffs and judgment.

4. Build a two-page SES resume you can tailor when the vacancy opens

Draft a two-page resume around your target role. Put your most relevant accomplishments where they’re easy to find. Include the federal job details the announcement requests, such as series and grade where applicable. USAJOBS limits resumes uploaded or built on the platform to two pages. Check the vacancy’s Qualifications, Required Documents, and How to Apply sections for how to demonstrate ECQs and technical qualifications and what supporting material to submit. Read the USAJOBS federal resume guidance.

Keep a separate record of the accomplishments that didn’t fit. Once the vacancy opens, you can swap in stronger evidence for that specific role, check every required document, and prepare interview examples from the same set of verified accomplishments.

5. Decide what kind of SES resume help you need

If you already have a draft and plan to revise it yourself, my SES Strategy & Review package gives you written feedback on how well your experience aligns with the target role and where the evidence needs to be stronger. You handle the revisions and formatting.

If you want me to write and format the two-page document, my SES Resume & CCAR package includes hands-on resume development and concise leadership examples. The Complete SES Application package is for candidates who want broader support, including technical qualification material when the vacancy calls for it and preparation for the SES interview.

If you have a draft, bring it along with the announcement you’re targeting or a comparable posting. That gives us a starting point for deciding which package fits. Ask me about SES resume review and writing services at Transformations123.

Position Yourself for What Comes Next

At Transformations123, I help mid-level and senior government, military, and corporate leaders position their experience for private-sector leadership and executive opportunities. My services include executive career strategy, leadership positioning, executive resume development, LinkedIn personal branding, and executive interview preparation.

The work begins by identifying where your experience creates the greatest value and developing a compelling professional narrative around that value. Because your goal is not simply to have a better resume. Your goal is to be recognized as a leader who can deliver value in your next organization.

If you are preparing for a government-to-private-sector transition, a military-to-civilian executive career, or your next corporate leadership opportunity, your experience deserves a strategy that reflects its full potential.
